title: Journey to the Centre of the Earth
subtitle: Layers, plates, quakes, volcanoes and the giant magnet under your feet
subject: Earth

p: People have walked on the Moon, 384,000 kilometres away. Nobody has been more than 4 kilometres under the ground. The centre of the Earth is 6,371 kilometres below your feet, and no drill has come close. The deepest hole ever made is in Russia. It took 20 years to dig and reached 12 kilometres. That is only one fifth of one percent of the way down.

Why did they stop? It got too hot. At the bottom of the hole the rock was 180 degrees Celsius, so hot and soft that the drill could no longer cut it. Everything we know about the deep Earth comes from clever detective work, not from going there.
pages.cap: We have mapped the surface of Earth from space, but the inside is still mostly a mystery.
pages.fact: Did you know? If Earth were the size of an apple, the deepest hole ever dug would not even scratch the skin.

p: Earth is built in layers. The outside is the crust, the thin rocky shell we live on. Under the oceans it is only about 7 kilometres thick. Under the continents it is about 35 kilometres. If Earth were an apple, the crust would be thinner than the apple's skin.

Below the crust is the mantle, a layer of hot rock 2,900 kilometres deep. It holds more than 80 percent of Earth's bulk. Under that is the outer core, a sea of liquid iron and nickel 2,200 kilometres thick. At the very centre sits the inner core, a solid iron ball about 2,440 kilometres across. That is about two thirds the size of the Moon.
pages.cap: Crust, mantle, outer core, inner core: the deeper you go, the hotter and heavier it gets.
pages.fact: Did you know? The inner core is about 5,400 degrees Celsius, as hot as the surface of the Sun, yet it stays solid because of the crushing pressure.

pages.h: How do we know what is inside?
p: You can tell if a melon is ripe by tapping it and listening. Scientists do the same with Earth, but the tap is an earthquake. Every big quake sends waves through the whole planet. Machines on the other side record when they arrive. One type of wave travels at about 6 kilometres per second through the crust and speeds up in denser rock.

Another type cannot pass through liquid at all. In the early 1900s, scientists noticed these waves vanished on the far side of Earth. The only explanation was a liquid layer deep inside. In 1936 a Danish scientist named Inge Lehmann studied the waves even more carefully and found a solid ball inside the liquid: the inner core.
pages.cap: Earthquake waves travel through the planet the way sound travels through a melon, and they change speed in each layer.
pages.fact: Did you know? A large earthquake makes the whole Earth ring like a bell for days, too slowly for anyone to hear.

pages.h: The centre of the Earth is as hot as the surface of the Sun
p: About 5,400 degrees Celsius. Yet the inner core is solid iron, because the weight of the whole planet presses down on it.

pages.q: Which layer of the Earth is liquid?
pages.why: The outer core is a sea of melted iron and nickel. Scientists know because one kind of earthquake wave, which cannot cross liquid, disappears when it reaches that layer.

p: The mantle is solid rock, but it is so hot that over thousands of years it slowly flows, like very thick toffee or the glacier of a mountain. Heat from the core warms the bottom of the mantle. Hot rock is lighter, so it rises. Near the top it cools, gets heavier and sinks again. This slow circle is called convection.

You have seen convection in a pot of soup on the stove. Hot soup rises in the middle and sinks at the edges. In the mantle the same thing happens, but the rock moves only a few centimetres a year. One full loop from bottom to top and back can take 100 million years. That slow stirring moves whole continents.
pages.cap: Heat rising from the core stirs the mantle like soup in a pot, only millions of times slower.

p: Earth's crust is not one piece. It is cracked into about 15 giant slabs called tectonic plates, seven of them huge. They float on the soft, slowly moving mantle beneath. Canada and the United States ride on the North American plate. As the mantle churns, the plates get dragged along.

How fast? Between 2 and 10 centimetres a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. The Atlantic Ocean widens by about 2.5 centimetres every year, so North America and Europe are slowly drifting apart. That is too slow to feel, but keep it up for 100 million years and an ocean appears where there was none.
pages.cap: Earth's surface is a jigsaw of moving plates that bump, slide and pull apart.
pages.fact: Did you know? Satellites can now measure plate movement to within a millimetre a year.

p: Look at a map. The east coast of South America fits the west coast of Africa like two puzzle pieces. In 1912 a German scientist named Alfred Wegener said the continents had once been joined. He found matching rock layers and fossils of the same land animals on both sides of the Atlantic. Most scientists laughed. Nobody could explain how continents could move.

Fifty years later, maps of the ocean floor proved him right. About 300 million years ago all the land was one supercontinent called Pangaea. It cracked apart around 200 million years ago. Continents float on the mantle a bit like icebergs float on the sea, with deep roots hidden below.
pages.cap: Like an iceberg, a continent has far more rock hidden below than showing above.
pages.fact: Did you know? Fossils of the same reptile, Mesosaurus, are found only in Brazil and southern Africa. It could not swim across an ocean.

pages.h: Try it: see the mantle move
p: Watch convection happen in a glass.
steps: Fill a clear glass or jar with cold water and let it sit still for a minute.
Ask an adult to fill a small cup with very hot tap water and add several drops of food colouring.
Using a spoon, slowly lower a little of the hot coloured water into the bottom of the cold glass.
Watch. The warm colour rises to the top, spreads out, cools and sinks. That is exactly what hot rock does in the mantle, only millions of times slower.
pages.cap: Warm coloured water rises and spreads just like hot rock in the mantle.
pages.safe: Hot water can scald. Let an adult handle it.

p: About 50 million years ago the plate carrying India crashed into Asia. Neither side would sink, so the land crumpled upward like the hood of a car in a crash. The crumple is the Himalayas, home to Mount Everest, 8,849 metres tall. India is still pushing, so the mountains grow about 5 millimetres every year.

Here is the strange part. Near the top of Everest, climbers find rocks packed with fossils of sea creatures. The highest point on Earth was once the floor of an ocean. The crash lifted it 8 kilometres into the sky. Most big mountain ranges on Earth were made by plates pushing together.
pages.cap: Two plates collide and the crust buckles upward, building mountains over millions of years.

p: Plates do not only collide. Down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean runs a 16,000 kilometre crack where two plates pull apart. Hot rock rises to fill the gap and makes new sea floor. Iceland sits right on this crack. The island is being split in two and grows about 2 centimetres wider every year.

In California, two plates slide past each other along the San Andreas Fault. The western side, carrying Los Angeles, creeps north by about 5 centimetres a year. In roughly 15 million years Los Angeles will be next to San Francisco. The plates do not slide smoothly, though. They stick, then jerk. Each jerk is an earthquake.
pages.cap: Iceland is built from lava that rose up through the crack where two plates pull apart.
pages.fact: Did you know? In Iceland you can walk through a valley with North America on one side and Europe on the other.

pages.q: How fast do most tectonic plates move?
opts: About as fast as your fingernails grow
About as fast as you walk
About as fast as a car
pages.why: Plates move 2 to 10 centimetres a year, about the speed of growing fingernails. Over millions of years that adds up to whole oceans.

p: Plates want to move, but their rough edges catch and stick. For years, even centuries, the pressure builds while the rock bends like a stick. Then it snaps. The stored energy bursts out as waves that shake the ground. That is an earthquake. The spot where the rock breaks is the focus, and the point above it on the surface is the epicentre.

Earth has about 500,000 earthquakes every year. People feel around 100,000 of them. Only about 100 cause damage. Most are small jolts along plate edges. Machines called seismometers record them all. The oldest design used a heavy hanging weight. The ground shakes, but the weight stays still, so a pen attached to it draws the shaking.
pages.cap: A seismometer uses a heavy hanging weight that stays still while the ground shakes under it.

p: Scientists give every earthquake a magnitude number. The scale is tricky. Each step up means about 32 times more energy. A magnitude 5 is not a little bigger than a 4, it is 32 times bigger. A magnitude 7 releases about 1,000 times the energy of a 5. The strongest ever recorded was a magnitude 9.5 in Chile in 1960.

A magnitude 3 feels like a truck rumbling past. A 6 knocks pictures off walls and cracks old buildings. An 8 can flatten a city. Luckily big ones are rare. In a typical year Earth has about 13,000 quakes of magnitude 4, around 15 of magnitude 7, and just one of magnitude 8 or more.
pages.cap: Big quakes are rare. For every magnitude 8 there are about 13,000 of magnitude 4.
pages.fact: Did you know? Japan has so many quakes that children practise earthquake drills the way Canadian children practise fire drills.

pages.h: Tsunami: the wave from the deep
p: When a big quake happens under the sea, the ocean floor can jump up by several metres. It shoves the whole column of water above it, and a wave spreads out in every direction. In the deep ocean a tsunami is only about 1 metre high but hundreds of kilometres long, and it travels at 800 kilometres per hour. A ship can pass over one without noticing.

Near the coast the water gets shallow and the wave slows down. The water behind piles up on the water in front, and the wave grows. Some have reached 30 metres, taller than a nine-storey building. If you are ever at a beach and the sea suddenly pulls far back, run to high ground. A tsunami may be minutes away.
pages.cap: Far out at sea a boat barely notices a tsunami pass underneath. Near shore the same wave can tower over houses.
pages.fact: Did you know? Tsunami is a Japanese word meaning harbour wave, because fishermen at sea saw nothing but came home to a wrecked harbour.

pages.h: A tsunami crosses the ocean as fast as a jet plane
p: About 800 kilometres per hour in deep water. A wave made off Japan can reach Canada's west coast in under 10 hours.

pages.q: How tall is a tsunami in the deep ocean?
pages.why: Out at sea a tsunami is low but very long and very fast. It only grows tall when it reaches shallow water near the coast and the water piles up.

p: Deep in the crust, rock sometimes melts into a glowing mush called magma. Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it rises, like a bubble in honey. Where it finds a crack, it pushes up to the surface. Once it comes out, we call it lava. A volcano is a hill of hardened lava and ash with a pipe to the magma below.

Why do some volcanoes explode? Magma holds gas, like a fizzy drink. As it rises, the pressure drops and the bubbles swell. Thick, sticky magma traps them until they burst out in one blast. Runny magma lets the gas escape gently, so the lava just oozes. Earth has about 1,500 volcanoes that could erupt, and about 50 do each year.
pages.cap: Hot magma rises through a pipe in the crust and bursts out as lava, ash and gas.
pages.fact: Did you know? Lava is between 700 and 1,200 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt aluminium.

p: Draw a line around the edge of the Pacific Ocean: up the coast of South and North America, across to Japan and down through Indonesia and New Zealand. About three quarters of the world's volcanoes sit on that line, the Ring of Fire. Here, ocean plates dive under other plates and melt, feeding volcanoes above.

Hawaii is different. It sits in the middle of a plate, above a hot spot where extra-hot rock rises from deep in the mantle. As the plate slides over the hot spot, it leaves a chain of islands behind. Measured from the sea floor, Mauna Loa is more than 9 kilometres tall, higher than Everest. The biggest volcano we know is not on Earth. Olympus Mons on Mars is 22 kilometres high.
pages.cap: Mauna Loa from the sea floor is 9 kilometres tall. Olympus Mons on Mars is 22.

p: In the year 79, Mount Vesuvius buried the Roman town of Pompeii in hot ash so fast that bread was left in the ovens. In 1815 Tambora in Indonesia blew out so much ash and gas that it dimmed the Sun around the world. The next year, 1816, was called the year without a summer. Crops failed and it snowed in June in parts of North America.

In 1883 Krakatoa exploded with the loudest sound in recorded history. People heard it 4,800 kilometres away. In 1980 Mount St Helens in Washington state blew off its top 400 metres in a few minutes. In 2022 an undersea volcano near Tonga shot a cloud 57 kilometres high, the tallest ever measured.

pages.cap: Five eruptions that people around the world still talk about.
pages.fact: Did you know? Pumice is lava so full of gas bubbles that it floats. After Tonga erupted, rafts of pumice drifted across the Pacific.

p: Make gas bubbles push liquid out of a cone, just like a real eruption.
steps: Stand a small plastic bottle in a baking tray and build a cone of damp sand or modelling clay around it, leaving the top open.
Pour in 2 spoonfuls of baking soda, a squirt of dish soap and a few drops of red food colouring.
Pour in half a cup of vinegar and step back. The gas made by the mixture pushes the foam up and out, the way gas pushes lava out of a volcano.
Try again with a thicker mix, like adding a spoonful of flour to the vinegar. Does it ooze or burst?
pages.cap: Gas bubbles do the pushing, in your bottle and inside a real volcano.
pages.safe: Keep the mixture away from eyes and wipe up spills. Do this outside or on a tray.

p: Hold a compass anywhere on Earth and the needle swings to point north. Why? The outer core is a 2,200 kilometre deep ocean of liquid iron, and it is swirling. Earth's spin twists these flows into huge loops. Moving liquid metal makes electricity, and electricity makes magnetism. The whole planet becomes one enormous bar magnet.

The magnetic north pole is not at the true North Pole. It sits in the Arctic Ocean, drifting from Canada toward Siberia, and it wanders about 40 kilometres a year as the iron currents shift. Earth's magnetic field reaches more than 60,000 kilometres out into space, nearly five times farther than the planet is wide.
pages.cap: Swirling liquid iron in the outer core turns the whole planet into a bar magnet with north and south poles.
pages.fact: Did you know? Earth's magnetic field has flipped many times. The last time north became south was about 780,000 years ago.

p: The Sun blows out a constant storm of charged particles called the solar wind. Without protection, it would slowly strip away our air and water. Earth's magnetic field bends the wind around the planet like a boulder splitting a river. Some particles sneak in near the poles, hit the air and make it glow. That glow is the aurora, the northern lights.

Mars lost most of its magnetic field about 4 billion years ago. Over time the solar wind blew away most of its air, and its rivers and lakes dried up. Earth kept its shield and kept its oceans. Birds, sea turtles and even some bacteria can sense the field and use it like a built-in compass.
pages.cap: Mars lost its magnetic shield and then lost most of its air and water.
pages.fact: Did you know? Stripes of magnetised rock on the sea floor record every flip of Earth's field, like a tape recorder.

opts: Swirling liquid iron in the outer core
The Moon pulling on the planet
pages.why: Moving liquid iron in the outer core makes electric currents, and electric currents make magnetism. That turns Earth into one giant magnet.

p: Every rock on Earth belongs to one of three families. Igneous rock is frozen magma. Granite cooled slowly underground and has big sparkly crystals. Basalt cooled fast on the surface and is dark and fine. Pumice cooled so fast around gas bubbles that it floats on water.

Sedimentary rock is made from bits. Sand, mud and shells settle at the bottom of seas and lakes, layer upon layer, and are squeezed into stone over millions of years. Sandstone and limestone are examples, and almost every fossil is found in them. Metamorphic rock is rock that was cooked and squeezed deep in the crust until it changed. Limestone becomes marble. Mud rock becomes slate.
pages.cap: Sedimentary layers stack up like pages in a book, with the oldest at the bottom.

p: Rock is always being recycled. Mountains wear down into sand. Sand becomes sandstone. Sandstone gets dragged deep, cooked into metamorphic rock, melted into magma and erupted as lava again. This loop is called the rock cycle, and one lap can take hundreds of millions of years.

Because of this, very old rock is rare. Earth is 4.54 billion years old, but the oldest rock ever found is about 4 billion years old. It is in the Northwest Territories of Canada. Diamonds are the deepest rocks you can hold. They form more than 150 kilometres down and ride to the surface in very fast, very old volcanic eruptions.
pages.cap: Dinosaur bones are found only in sedimentary rock, laid down layer by layer while the dinosaurs lived.
pages.fact: Did you know? The oldest known piece of Earth is a zircon crystal from Australia, 4.4 billion years old and smaller than a grain of sand.

p: Where does all the heat inside Earth come from? About half is left over from when the planet formed from crashing rocks 4.5 billion years ago. The other half comes from tiny amounts of radioactive elements in the rock that give off heat as they slowly break down. Earth is cooling, but so slowly that it has barely changed in a billion years.

People put that heat to use. In Iceland, hot rock near the surface heats water for about 90 percent of all homes, and steam from the ground spins turbines for electricity. Hot springs in Canada's Rocky Mountains are rain that sank deep, touched hot rock and rose back up. The ground 3 kilometres down is already around 100 degrees Celsius almost anywhere on Earth.
pages.cap: Rain sinks through cracks, meets hot rock and comes back up as a hot spring or a geyser.
